step1.title: Spot the Bivalue Pattern
step1.description: Look at the unsolved cells on this puzzle. Almost every single one has exactly TWO candidates. This is a very special situation called a 'Bivalue Universal Grave' (BUG). Here's why it's a problem: if EVERY unsolved cell had exactly two candidates arranged in a certain pattern, you could swap the values around and get two different valid solutions! But a proper Sudoku puzzle has only ONE solution. So something must 'break' this pattern - there must be at least one cell that's different.

step2.title: Find the Exception Cell
step2.description: Now look at {{cell}} - this cell is special! While all the other unsolved cells have exactly two candidates, this one has THREE (or more). This is the 'plus one' in BUG+1. This extra candidate is the key to solving the puzzle. If we removed this extra candidate, we'd have the deadly BUG pattern with multiple solutions. Therefore, the extra candidate MUST be the true value of this cell!

step3.title: Prevent the BUG
step3.description: To avoid the BUG (which would mean multiple solutions), we must eliminate the candidates that would complete the deadly pattern. Remove {{digits}} from {{cell}}. The remaining candidate is the solution for this cell.

step1.title: Find the Chain
step1.description: An Alternating Inference Chain (AIC) connects candidates in a logical sequence. Think of it like a chain of dominoes where each piece affects the next. This chain has {{nodeCount}} links, starting at {{startDesc}} and ending at {{endDesc}}. The chain alternates between two types of connections: • **Strong links** (solid lines): 'If this is FALSE, then that must be TRUE' • **Weak links** (dashed lines): 'If this is TRUE, then that must be FALSE'. By following the chain, we can prove certain candidates must be eliminated.

step2.title: Follow the Logic

step3.title: Make the Elimination
step3.description: The chain proves that {{digits}} cannot be in {{cells}}. Why? Because the chain's endpoints create a 'trap': no matter which endpoint is true, the elimination cell would see a cell that has the candidate. Remove {{digits}} from: {{cells}}.

step1.title: Understand Almost Locked Sets
step1.description: An **Almost Locked Set** (ALS) is a group of cells that's 'almost' solved. Here's the key idea: if you have N cells containing exactly N+1 different candidates, then removing just ONE candidate would 'lock' the remaining candidates to those cells. For example: 3 cells with candidates {1,2,3,4} = almost locked. Remove any one digit, and the other 3 digits MUST go in those 3 cells. This {{alsType}} technique uses {{numALS}} Almost Locked Sets that share 'connecting digits' - digits that can only be in one ALS or the other, linking them together.

Look at {{alsName}}: {{cellCount}} cells ({{cells}}) with {{digitCount}} candidates {{{digits}}}. This is {{cellCount}} cells with {{digitCount}} candidates - that's 'almost locked' because {{digitCount}} = {{cellCount}} + 1.

step1.title: Find the Connecting Digits
Make the Elimination
step1.description: Now for the payoff! Look at the digit(s) {{digits}}. Because of how the ALSs are connected, {{digits}} must end up in one of the ALS cells. Any cell that can 'see' ALL the places where {{digits}} could be in BOTH ALSs cannot have {{digits}} - it would always conflict. Remove {{digits}} from: {{cells}}.

step1.title: Find the X-Cycle
step1.description: An X-Cycle is a chain of cells that loops back to where it started. This cycle has {{cycleSize}} nodes involving digit {{digit}} at cells: {{cells}}. The key is that the chain alternates between 'strong links' (solid lines) and 'weak links' (dashed lines). Strong link = if one is false, the other must be true. Weak link = both cannot be true at the same time. Because the chain forms a complete loop, certain candidates MUST be eliminated to avoid a contradiction.

step3.title: Eliminate from Cells Seeing Both Colors
step3.description: The cell(s) at {{cells}} can see nodes of both 'colors' in the cycle. Since one color must be true, these cells would always conflict. Remove {{digit}} from: {{cells}}.

step1.description: This is a 'Nice Loop' (even number of nodes). In a nice loop, we can color the nodes alternately - let's call them 'Green' and 'Yellow'. All green nodes would have {{digit}}, OR all yellow nodes would have {{digit}}. Any cell that can see BOTH a green and a yellow node cannot have {{digit}} - no matter which color is true, that cell would conflict with it.

This is a 'Discontinuous Loop' (odd number of nodes). With an odd cycle, something must 'break' - we find a contradiction. Following the chain logic, we can prove certain candidates must be eliminated because keeping them would create an impossible situation.

step1.title: Understand Simple Coloring
step1.description: Simple Coloring works on a single digit ({{digit}}). Here's the idea: Find all the 'strong links' for digit {{digit}}. A strong link exists when {{digit}} appears in exactly two cells of a row, column, or box - if one is false, the other must be true. Now color these cells alternately - start with 'Green', connected cells become 'Yellow', their connections become 'Green' again, and so on. We have {{greenCount}} Green cells and {{yellowCount}} Yellow cells. Either ALL green cells have {{digit}}, OR ALL yellow cells have {{digit}}.

step1.title: Understand 3D Medusa Coloring
step1.description: 3D Medusa extends coloring to multiple digits. Here's the idea: Start with any candidate and call it 'Green'. Every candidate connected by a strong link gets the opposite color ('Yellow'). Strong links exist when: • A digit appears only twice in a row, column, or box • A cell has only two candidates (bivalue cell). We color {{greenCount}} cells Green and {{yellowCount}} cells Yellow. One entire color group is TRUE, the other is FALSE - we just don't know which yet.

step2.title: Find Color Traps and Wraps
step2.description: Now we look for contradictions or 'traps': **Color Trap**: If an uncolored cell can see both a Green and a Yellow cell (in the same row, column, or box), that cell cannot have the digit. Why? Because one of those colors must be true, and either would eliminate the digit from that cell. **Color Wrap**: If two cells of the SAME color can see each other, that color is impossible! They can't both have the digit. So the OTHER color must be entirely true.

step3.title: Make the Elimination
step3.description: Based on the coloring analysis: The cell(s) at {{cells}} either see both colors (Color Trap) or are part of a color that contradicts itself (Color Wrap). Remove the candidate(s) from: {{cells}}.

step1.title: Spot the Deadly Pattern
step1.description: Look at these four cells forming a rectangle: {{cells}}. They span exactly two rows, two columns, and two boxes. Notice they all contain the candidates {{digits}}. Here's the problem: if these four cells ONLY had {{digits}} as candidates, you could swap the digits between the diagonal corners and still have a valid solution! That means the puzzle would have TWO solutions - which is not allowed in proper Sudoku. This forbidden pattern is called a 'Deadly Pattern' or 'Unique Rectangle'.

step1.title: Understand Type {{type}}
step1.description: This is Type 1 - the simplest case. Three corners of the rectangle have only {{digits}}, but {{extraCell}} has an extra candidate. Think about it: if {{extraCell}} were just {{digits}} like the others, we'd have the deadly pattern. So the extra candidate MUST be the true value of that cell! We can safely remove {{digits}} from {{extraCell}}.

step1.title: Understand Type {{type}}
step1.description: This is Type 2 - two corners share the same extra candidate ({{extraDigit}}). These two cells are on opposite corners of the rectangle. Since the deadly pattern can't exist, at least one of these corners must be {{extraDigit}}. Any cell that can see BOTH of these corners cannot have {{extraDigit}}.

step1.title: Understand Type {{type}}
step1.description: This is Type 3 - two corners have extra candidates that form a 'naked subset' with nearby cells. The extra candidates in the UR corners, combined with other cells in the same house, force certain eliminations. The deadly pattern is avoided because the subset logic guarantees the UR won't complete.

step1.title: Understand Type {{type}}
step1.description: This is Type 4 - one of the UR digits ({{digits}}) is 'locked' into two opposite corners. Because of a strong link, one digit must go in those two corners. This means the OTHER digit cannot be in those corners (or we'd have the deadly pattern). Remove the non-locked digit from the locked corners.

step1.title: Understand Type {{type}}
step1.description: This is Type 5 - a diagonal strong link prevents the deadly pattern. Two opposite corners are strongly linked on one digit, meaning one of them must have it. This breaks the symmetry that would allow the deadly pattern.

step1.title: Understand Type {{type}}
step1.description: This is Type 6 - both diagonals have strong links on the same digit. This double-lock on one digit means it must appear in exactly two opposite corners, forcing the other digit out of those corners.

step1.title: Break the Pattern
step1.description: To avoid this deadly pattern, we need to ensure it can never complete. Something must 'break' the rectangle - either an extra candidate that must be true, or a strong link that forces one digit into specific corners.
Remove {{digits}} from {{cells}}. The extra candidate in this cell must be its true value to prevent the deadly pattern.

step1.title: Find the Empty Rectangle
step1.description: Look at {{box}}. The candidate {{digit}} only appears in an 'L-shape' or 'bent' pattern - it's missing from at least one row AND one column within the box. This creates an 'Empty Rectangle' - the empty row and column form a cross inside the box, and all the {{digit}} candidates are in the corners of this cross. The cells with {{digit}} are: {{cells}}.

step2.title: Connect to the Strong Link
step2.description: Now look outside the box. There's a 'strong link' (solid line) on {{digit}} at {{conjugateCells}}. A strong link means: if one end is false, the other MUST be true. One end of this strong link connects to the Empty Rectangle through a shared row or column. This creates a chain of logic: if the far end of the strong link is true, it eliminates {{digit}} from the intersection point in the box, which then forces {{digit}} to a different position in the ER.

step3.title: Make the Elimination
step3.description: Here's the key insight: the elimination cell ({{cells}}) can see both ends of our chain - it sees one end of the strong link AND it sees where {{digit}} would be forced in the Empty Rectangle. No matter which way the logic goes, {{digit}} will end up in a cell that sees {{cells}}. So {{digit}} cannot be in {{cells}}. Remove {{digit}} from: {{cells}}.

step1.title: Find the Two Strong Links
step1.description: A Skyscraper is a pattern with two **strong links** on the same digit. Look at {{baseNamesText}}. In each of these {{baseTypeText}}, digit {{digit}} appears in exactly TWO cells. That's a strong link - if one cell doesn't have {{digit}}, the other MUST have it. The two strong links are connected: one end of each strong link shares the same column (or row). The other ends - the 'roof' of the skyscraper (shown in yellow) - are the key cells.

step2.title: Follow the Logic
step2.description: Here's why the Skyscraper works: The connected ends of the two strong links are in the same column/row. If {{digit}} is NOT in one of the connected cells, the strong link forces it to be in that cell's partner. But that partner is the 'roof' cell! So no matter what: either {{digit}} is in one roof cell, or it's in the other roof cell (or possibly both). One of the roof cells MUST have {{digit}}.

step3.title: Eliminate from Cells Seeing Both Roofs
step3.description: Any cell that can see BOTH roof cells cannot have {{digit}}. Why? Because one of the roof cells must have {{digit}}, and that would eliminate {{digit}} from any cell seeing it. Since the elimination cell sees both roof cells, it will always be eliminated. Remove {{digit}} from: {{cells}}.

step1.title: Find the Finned Pattern
step1.description: This is a **Finned {{fishType}}**. Let's start with the basic pattern: Look at {{baseNames}}. In a normal {{fishType}}, digit {{digit}} would appear only in cells that align with {{coverNames}}. But here, there's an extra cell (or cells) that doesn't fit - that's the 'fin'. The fin is at: {{finCells}} (shown in yellow).

step2.title: Understand the Fin's Effect
step2.description: The fin changes what we can eliminate. Here's the logic: **If the fin is TRUE** (has {{digit}}): The normal fish pattern applies to the rest, but we can only eliminate from cells that ALSO see the fin. **If the fin is FALSE**: Then {{digit}} must be somewhere else in the fish pattern, and the normal fish eliminations would apply. Either way, any cell that sees both the fin AND the fish pattern can be eliminated! This means eliminations are restricted to {{boxName}} (where the fin is).

step3.title: Eliminate Where Fin and Fish Meet
step3.description: Cells that can see the fin AND are in the fish's cover lines can be eliminated. These cells are in {{boxName}} (so they see the fin) and also in one of the cover {{coverTypeText}} (so the fish pattern affects them). Remove {{digit}} from: {{cells}}.

step1.description: Look at the yellow cell at {{pivotName}} - it's called the 'hinge' and has exactly two candidates. Now look at the two green cells at {{pincerNamesText}} - these are the 'pincers'. Each pincer shares one candidate with the hinge, but they both have {{targetDigitText}} in common. Here's the key: no matter which candidate goes in the hinge, one of the pincers MUST end up with {{targetDigitText}}.

step2.title: Understand why it works
step2.description: Since one pincer MUST have {{targetDigitText}}, any cell that can see BOTH pincers cannot have {{targetDigitText}}. It would conflict with whichever pincer ends up with that digit. The solid line shows that one pincer must be true for {{targetDigitText}}.

step1.title: Find the {{wingType}} pattern
step1.description: Look at the yellow cell at {{pivotName}} - it has three candidates: {{wingDigitText}}. The two green cells at {{pincerNamesText}} each share two of those candidates with the hinge. The digit {{targetDigitText}} appears in ALL three cells. Since every outcome forces {{targetDigitText}} into one of these cells, any cell that can see all three cannot have {{targetDigitText}}.

step1.title: Find the {{wingType}} pattern
step1.description: Look at the two green cells at {{pincerNamesText}}. They both have the same two candidates. These cells are connected by a 'strong link' (shown as a solid line) on one of those digits. This means: if the linking digit is removed from one cell, the other cell MUST have it. Either way, one of these cells will have {{targetDigitText}}.

step2.title: Understand why it works
step2.description: Because the two cells are connected by a strong link, their 'other' candidate ({{targetDigitText}}) is restricted. Any cell seeing both green cells would conflict with whichever one ends up with {{targetDigitText}}.

step1.title: Find the kite pattern
step1.description: Look at the two green {{digit}} candidates at {{kiteNames}}. These are the endpoints of the kite. They're connected through {{coverNames}}, which contains two more {{digit}} candidates (shown in yellow). Think of it like this: one of the green cells MUST have {{digit}}, but they can't BOTH have it.

step2.title: Follow the chain
step2.description: The kite forms a chain: {{chain}}. The solid lines indicate strong links, and the dashed line indicates a weak link. No matter which green cell has {{digit}}, the weak link ensures that at least one of the yellow cells in the box will have it. Any cell that can see BOTH green cells at {{kiteNames}} cannot have {{digit}}.

step3.description: Since {{cells}} can see both green cells, we know {{digit}} cannot go there. Eliminate {{digit}} from: {{cells}}.
